01 / GET TO KNOW PLAIN

A language with
room to grow.

Plain is a high-level programming language created by MR-CODESPIKE. Its syntax takes inspiration from classic, readable languages, while its compiler uses LLVM to generate native machine code.

You can start with variables and decisions, then move into functions, collections, classes, error handling, file operations and machine-learning integrations.

✳

One important distinction: Plain's values are dynamically typed at runtime. Type annotations can help the compiler check certain things, but they do not turn the language into a fully static type system.

⌘

Clear syntax

Keywords such as LET, IF, REPEAT and SAY make the shape of a program easy to follow.

03 / CHAPTER ONE — FOUNDATIONS

Your first
Plain program.

A program is a set of instructions. Plain executes those instructions in order, from top to bottom, unless a control-flow statement changes the path.

Meet SAY

SAY writes a value to the program's output. It is the quickest way to see what your program is doing.

  • ✓ Text goes inside double quotes.
  • ✓ Each instruction can be on its own line.
  • ✓ A # begins a comment.

Read code from top to bottom

The first line prints a greeting. The second line prints a number. The third line is a comment, so it is not executed.

Ask the user for input

ASK reads input into a newly declared variable. Use a semicolon for a string input or a colon for an integer input.

ASK "Your name? "; name
SAY "Hello, " + name
ASK "Your age? ": age
✳ QUICK TIP

Comments are for people reading your code. Use them to explain why something happens, not just repeat what the code already says.

YOUR FIRST FILE
1 SAY "Hello, Plain!"
2 SAY 2026
3 # My first Plain program
EXPECTED OUTPUT
Hello, Plain!
2026
● EXAMPLE OUTPUT
04 / THE CORE BUILDING BLOCKS

Understand the
moving parts.

These are the ideas you will use in almost every program. Take your time with them: a strong foundation makes advanced code much easier to understand.

01
DATA & VALUES

Variables: give information a name

A variable is a named place in your program where you can refer to a value. In Plain, use LET to declare a variable. Use SET when you want to assign a new value to an existing variable.

LET username = "Ada"
LET points = 10
SET points = points + 5
SAY username
SAY points

What happens? username stores the text "Ada". points starts at 10, then SET changes it to 15.

Remember: Variables are block-scoped. A variable declared inside an IF, REPEAT, TRY or CATCH block is not visible after that block ends. Declare it before the block if you need it later.
VARIABLE BOX
username"Ada"
points10 → 15
↑ SET updates the value
02
DATA & VALUES

Types: different kinds of information

Plain values are dynamically typed. A value's kind matters when you operate on it. The common types are integers, floating-point numbers, booleans, strings, lists, dictionaries, errors and null.

123IntegerWhole numbers
3.14FloatDecimal numbers
TRUEBooleanTrue or false
"Hi"StringText characters
[ ]ListOrdered items
{ }DictionaryKey-value pairs

Type annotations such as LET age AS int = 18 can be checked at compile time where the compiler can see the types. They do not change runtime behaviour or make every variable statically typed.

LET age AS int = 18
LET price AS float = 2.5
LET is_ready = TRUE
LET tags = ["plain", "learn"]
SAY TYPE_OF(age)
VALUE
123"abc"TRUE[ ]{ }
03
DATA & VALUES

Operators: make values work together

Operators perform calculations and comparisons. If either arithmetic operand is a float, Plain performs the operation in floating point. Integer division truncates toward zero.

Math+ - * / %Add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder
Compare= != < <= > >=Compare numbers or strings
LogicAND OR NOTCombine or invert conditions
SAY 7 + 3       # 10
SAY 7 / 2       # 3 (integer division)
SAY 7.0 / 2     # 3.5
SAY 5 > 2       # TRUE
Integer arithmetic uses 64-bit two's-complement values and wraps on overflow. Division or modulo by zero produces an error value.
04
DATA & VALUES

Lists & dictionaries: organise your data

A list stores an ordered sequence of items. A dictionary stores values under keys. They let you group related information instead of creating a separate variable for every item.

LET colours = ["orange", "black"]
APPEND(colours, "white")
SAY colours[0]

LET person = {name: "Mina", age: 20}
SAY person["name"]
SAY KEYS(person)

List indexes start at zero, so the first item is at index 0. Dictionaries map keys to values. The standard library includes helpers such as APPEND, REMOVE, SORT, SUM, KEYS and VALUES.

LIST · colours
0"orange"
1"black"
2"white"+ appended
DICTIONARY · person
name"Mina"
age20
05 / CONTROL THE FLOW

Choose a path.
Repeat with purpose.

Control flow determines which instructions run and how often. Plain uses readable block endings so you can see where each decision or loop begins and ends.

⇄

IF / ELSE

Run one block when a condition is true, and optionally another block when it is false. Close the structure with END IF.

IF score >= 50 THEN
    SAY "Passed"
ELSE
    SAY "Try again"
END IF
condition↙TRUEFALSE↘two possible paths
⟳

REPEAT

Repeat a block. A counted loop uses FROM and TO; both endpoints are included. A condition-controlled loop uses REPEAT WHILE condition and keeps going while the condition remains true.

REPEAT i FROM 1 TO 3
    SAY i
END REPEAT
1→2→3↺
↪

FOR EACH

Visit each item in a collection once. This is useful when you do not need to manage indexes yourself.

LET names = ["Ada", "Lin"]
REPEAT FOR EACH name IN names
    SAY name
END REPEAT
"Ada"→"Lin"✓
⚠
BREAK & CONTINUE

BREAK exits the current loop. CONTINUE skips to the next iteration. Both are compile errors when used outside a loop.

06 / REUSABLE LOGIC

Write once.
Call anywhere.

Functions give a name to a reusable block of instructions. They can accept parameters and send a result back to the caller.

Meet TO and GIVE BACK

Define a function using TO. Parameters are written inside parentheses. Use GIVE BACK to return a value. Close the function with END TO.

The optional GIVES annotation documents the intended return type and can be checked where the compiler can see the type.

FUNCTION TIP

Give functions names that describe the job they perform. calculate_total tells a reader more than do_thing.

GREETING.FUNCTION
1 TO greet(name AS string) GIVES string
2     GIVE BACK "Hello, " + name
3 END TO
4
5 LET message = greet("Ada")
6 SAY message
EXPECTED OUTPUT
Hello, Ada
● EXAMPLE OUTPUT
07 / OBJECT-ORIENTED PROGRAMMING

Describe things.
Build objects.

Classes let you define the shape and behaviour of objects. Plain supports fields, constructors, methods and inheritance.

Class, field, constructor, method

A CLASS groups data and behaviour. Fields describe the information each object carries. TO NEW is the constructor: it runs when you create an instance with NEW.

A child class can use EXTENDS to inherit from a parent class. Use SUPER.NEW(...) to call the parent constructor and SUPER.method() to call a parent method.

Every field receives its declared constant default or a type default before the constructor runs. Inherited fields are initialised before child fields.
CLASSAnimalname · legs
↑ EXTENDS
CLASSBirdinherits Animal
ANIMALS.PLAIN
1 CLASS Animal
2     LET name AS string
3     LET legs AS int = 4
4     TO NEW n AS string
5         SET name = n
6     END TO
7 END CLASS
8
9 LET dog = NEW Animal("Rex")
10 SAY dog.name
EXPECTED OUTPUT
Rex
● EXAMPLE OUTPUT
08 / LEVEL UP

Go beyond
the basics.

Real programs need to deal with failure, files and other systems. These features help you move from small examples to useful applications.

⚠

Error handling

Errors are values in Plain. Use TRY to watch a block for errors and CATCH to handle the first one.

TRY
    FAIL "Something went wrong"
CATCH err
    SAY ERROR_MESSAGE(err)
END TRY

FAIL is only allowed inside a function or a TRY block. Outside TRY, an error can flow as an ordinary value.

▤

Files & JSON

Read and write text files, inspect paths, and encode or decode JSON data using built-in functions.

LET data = {name: "Ada"}
LET json = JSON_ENCODE(data)
WRITE_FILE("person.json", json)
LET back = JSON_DECODE(json)

File functions work with the filesystem available to the running program. Treat untrusted programs carefully.

⌘

Modules & FFI

Use USE with a quoted Plain file path to import a module. Imported functions can then be called by their function names. The compiler also supports a foreign-function interface for compatible external functions.

USE "helpers.plain"
# Call a function defined in that file
SAY twice(21)

Imports are resolved relative to the entry file by default. External imports require explicit compiler configuration.

✳

Machine learning

The ecosystem includes a Rust-backed neural-network toolkit exposed through Plain's FFI layer.

# Explore the ML examples
# in the Plain Ecosystem repository
# and read docs/ML.md

It includes tensor operations, autograd, optimisation and classifier examples. It is an ecosystem library, not a built-in general AI model.

Core statements

LETDeclare a variable.

Decisions

ELSEAlternative branch.
END IFClose the conditional.
AND / OR / NOTBoolean logic.

Loops

REPEATStart a loop.
FOR EACHVisit each collection item.
BREAKExit the current loop.
CONTINUEMove to the next iteration.

Functions

TODefine a function or method.
GIVE BACKReturn a value.
GIVESAnnotate a return type.
END TOClose a function.

Classes

CLASSDefine a class.
EXTENDSInherit from a parent.
NEWCreate an instance.
SUPERAccess parent behaviour.

Errors

TRYBegin guarded execution.
CATCHHandle a caught error.
FAILCreate an error.
IS_ERRORCheck whether a value is an error.

String helpers

LENGTH(x)Count characters/items/keys.
UPPER(x)Upper-case text.
TRIM(x)Remove outside whitespace.
SPLIT(x, sep)Split text into a list.

Collection helpers

SORT(a)Return a sorted copy.

Math helpers
